analysis.one_liner: Permanently repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill sat in the Ways and Means Committee without ever getting a vote and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would erase the entire federal estate and gift tax system, including the tax on very large transfers that skip a generation, for everyone dying or giving gifts after 2002. Only estates above a size threshold ever owe the tax, so the money would go overwhelmingly to heirs of the largest estates. The bill never moved after being sent to the tax-writing committee, and it expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates gain the most, because the estate tax applies only to estates above the exemption amount — a few percent of all estates. Family businesses and farms that would otherwise face a tax bill at an owner's death would also be relieved of it. Wealthy households making very large lifetime gifts would no longer owe gift tax.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the estate tax, the gift tax, and the generation-skipping transfer tax for deaths and transfers after December 31, 2002.

Sponsor Rep. Christopher Cox and the bill's findings argue the tax forces families to pay 37 to 55 percent of after-tax savings at death and forces some small businesses and farms to sell assets to pay the bill.
The bill's findings state these transfer taxes produced about 1 percent of total federal revenues in fiscal year 2002, arguing repeal would cost the Treasury little while easing planning burdens.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury loses the revenue these taxes raise — roughly 1 percent of federal revenue per the bill's own findings — meaning the burden shifts to other taxpayers, to future borrowing, or to cuts elsewhere. The gains concentrate on the heirs of the very largest estates, since most estates owe nothing under the exemption thresholds.

drawbacks.text: Repeal permanently forgoes roughly 1 percent of federal revenue each year, which the bill's own findings acknowledge, and that revenue would have to come from other taxpayers or borrowing.

Because the tax only applies above the exemption threshold, the dollar value of repeal flows overwhelmingly to the largest estates rather than to typical families, making it a large tax cut concentrated at the top.

An honest supporter would concede that very few family farms and small businesses actually end up owing the tax once exemptions are applied, so the small-business argument covers a far broader tax cut than the hardship cases justify.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief for heirs is real but concentrated at the very top of the wealth distribution, while the revenue loss touches every taxpayer. The family-farm and small-business cases the bill leans on are the sympathetic face of a cut whose dollar benefits go mainly to the largest estates. As drafted, the bill offered no middle-ground option such as raising exemptions while keeping the tax at very high wealth levels.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Cox introduced the Family Heritage Preservation Act on January 7, 2003, the first day of the 108th Congress.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax law.
The bill text would repeal Subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code — the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes — effective for deaths and transfers after December 31, 2002.
Four Republicans cosponsored the bill; no further committees, floor action, or votes ever followed.
The bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, having never been reported out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury and ordinary taxpayers are better off, since the roughly 1 percent of federal revenue these taxes raise stayed on the books; heirs of the largest estates lost the chance at a permanent repeal.

for.name: Rep. Christopher Cox
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 108th Congress and wrote findings defending repeal of the estate and gift taxes.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Standing committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and never reported it, so it never reached the House floor.

against.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee action on the bill during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on; the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee declined to move it, and no votes were ever recorded.

industries.industry: Heirs of the largest estates and wealthy households
industries.note: Because the estate tax only applies above exemption thresholds, repeal's dollar benefit would flow almost entirely to the wealthiest families, and the roughly 1 percent of federal revenue it raises would shift to other taxpayers.

industries.industry: Estate planning attorneys and tax advisers
industries.note: The bill's own findings note families spend heavily on accountants and lawyers to structure trusts around the tax; repeal would eliminate much of that business, a loss that comes alongside a public gain in revenue.

industries.industry: Family farms and small business owners
industries.note: The bill targets cases where an heir must sell business or farm assets to pay the tax; a small number of such estates face this, and repeal would end it for all of them.
